question: Mr Sharma, a 60-year-old man, had an ischaemic stroke yesterday. He is haemodynamically stable with mild right-sided weakness (NIHSS 5). His family asks when physiotherapy should begin. What is the recommended timing for initiating stroke rehabilitation including early mobilisation?

answers.text: After 7 days — the brain needs at least a week of rest before any exertion.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no evidence supporting a 7-day rest period. Delayed mobilisation increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis, aspiration pneumonia, pressure sores, and muscle wasting.

answers.text: After 1 month — rehabilitation is only effective once the acute inflammatory response has resolved.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: One month is far too late. Early mobilisation within the first 24–48 hours is supported by strong evidence and guidelines. Waiting a month wastes the critical early recovery window.

answers.text: Within 24–48 hours of stroke onset, provided the patient is haemodynamically stable.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Early mobilisation within 24–48 hours is the strongest evidence-based principle in stroke rehabilitation. It reduces complications and harnesses the brain's early plasticity window. Haemodynamic stability is the key prerequisite.

answers.text: Only after formal neuropsychological assessment has been completed.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neuropsychological assessment is part of the rehabilitation process but is not a prerequisite to starting physical rehabilitation. Mobilisation can and should begin early, while other assessments proceed in parallel.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Timing and Phases of Stroke Rehabilitation block. The key takeaway: rehabilitation starts within 24–48 hours, not days or weeks. Delay incurs preventable complications and wastes neuroplasticity.

Well done. Early mobilisation (within 24–48 hours) is the cornerstone principle of stroke rehabilitation — safe, feasible, and strongly recommended for all haemodynamically stable stroke survivors with residual deficits.
